title: Price Check: Players Where Sites Disagree
brief: Which players have very different ranks or prices across sources, so their auction price in our room is hard to predict? Each line must say which direction the gap points and at what price the player becomes a buy for us.
summary: Yahoo, ESPN and last season's prices in our room often point in different directions. For us, expert value is the anchor and the cheaper market is the floor. Let others pay up for the Yahoo-inflated names (Cade Cunningham, Chet Holmgren, Trae Young) and the ESPN-inflated ones (Anthony Davis, Derrick White, Mikal Bridges). Spend the saved budget on players the experts rate well above their market cost, such as Matas Buzelis, Dejounte Murray, Damian Lillard and Paul George.

paragraphs.text: Rankings differ a lot between Yahoo, ESPN and Fantrax. Whether a player is a bust or a steal depends on the platform and format. We draft on Yahoo, but our managers read ESPN too. So for every player, check three numbers: the Yahoo average cost, the ESPN value and cost, and what our room paid last season.

Yahoo auction price data currently differs a lot from snake-draft ADP data. Keep the two apart. In an auction, use average auction cost to predict the room. Use snake ADP only as a rough guide to who the room thinks is a first or second rounder.

The widest gaps show the problem. Anthony Davis has an ESPN value about twice his Yahoo value, and he cost far more than either in our room last season. Naz Reid is a mid-round player on ESPN and a late one on Yahoo. Trae Young is a top-20 player on Yahoo and close to a throw-in on ESPN. For players like these, expect the room to split, and set your own ceiling before the draft.

sections.heading: Rank is quality, cost is the market

paragraphs.text: Rankings and projections measure quality. ADP and average cost show the market price. When you rate a player well above his market, buy him somewhere in between, not at your full rank. In auction terms: if the experts rate a player well above his average cost, bid above that cost but stop below the expert value.

This gives two groups. In one, the experts rate the player above every market, so he is a value at price. Matas Buzelis, Dejounte Murray, Damian Lillard and Paul George are examples. In the other, one market prices the player above the expert view. Let that price go to someone else. Cade Cunningham and Chet Holmgren on Yahoo, and Derrick White and Mikal Bridges on ESPN, are examples.

ADP is an average, not a median. A player with ADP 50 goes after pick 50 in only about half of drafts. Average auction cost works the same way. One manager who loves a player can pay well above it. Treat the average cost as the middle of the range, not as the ceiling.

The experts lean different ways on timing. One note says buy between your rank and the market price, which favours patience. Another says that when a player's ESPN ADP is far later than his rank, people keep passing on him, so grab him when that happens. A third warns that players often go earlier than their ADP suggests, so waiting can cost you the player. In our auction, wait on players whose market is still falling during the draft. For a player you rate far above his market, bid as soon as he is nominated rather than hoping he slips. Stop at the ceiling in his line.

A Yahoo ADP based on very few drafts can be inflated and misleading. Some Yahoo ADPs are also distorted by dynasty leagues, where a player is drafted in only a small share of leagues. Ignore those numbers. Before the draft, check how many drafts stand behind a Yahoo number. Trust it less when the player has no average cost or when the sources disagree on his rank.

Some players in our pool show these warning signs. Gui Santos and Danny Wolf have no Yahoo average cost. Russell Westbrook's ESPN rank differs between sources. Kelly Oubre Jr.'s Yahoo rank and his tag do not match. None of them should use one of our 144 draft spots. Leave them on waivers and watch their roles.

sections.heading: Do not anchor on last season's room

paragraphs.text: Last season our room paid far more than today's market and the experts suggest for several players. Examples are Anthony Davis, Devin Booker, Stephen Curry, Trae Young and Domantas Sabonis. Each of those prices bought a role or health picture that has changed, so do not repeat them.

The reverse also happened. Naz Reid, Keyonte George, Zach Edey and Nickeil Alexander-Walker went for 1 or 2 USD last season. The experts now value each of them at 10 USD or more. Expect someone in our room to know this, and plan to pay the expert range given in their lines.

For each split player, write down one ceiling before 2026-10-18 and stick to it. Clear up injury tags first: Bam Adebayo (groin, Q), Domantas Sabonis (Q) and Dejounte Murray (toe, Q). Near the end of the draft, the 144-player cutoff matters more than any site's rank. Players the experts rank around 120 to 165 are 1 USD picks at most, or waiver adds. Kristaps Porzingis and Andrew Nembhard are examples.
